newsitem.title: INDIA: India cyclone victims weep over ravaged farmland.
newsitem.headline: India cyclone victims weep over ravaged farmland.

text.p: People in Rawlapalam village wept on Saturday in homes devastated by a killer cyclone as vultures hovered over bloated cattle carcasses floating in canals swollen by flood waters.
The waters had receded from the village itself, leaving the snapped and jagged ends of once supple coconut trees sticking grotesquely into the sky, their fronds torn and crushed.
But the village in Andhra Pradesh state on India's southeast coast, set in lush greens field crisscrossed by canals and dotted with trees, was almost in ruins.
Many homes were open to the sky, their roofs blown off by winds up to 180 kmph (110 mph) late on Wednesday evening. The residents, farmers and fishermen, were hunting food and work.

Rawlapalam is one of more than 500 villages in East Godavari district that bore the brunt of the storm. Officials say the final death toll will be about 1,000 people, and in East Godavari alone the death count has passed 400.
"We all had an early dinner and went to sleep around 8 p.m. when a wind started blowing," said Lakshmi, a labourer.

"When it started picking up speed and started howling we got scared. I and my husband picked up our five children and a few belongings and moved into a brick and stone two-storey building close to our hut. We sensed there would be some trouble."
Lakshmi, 36, said the wind became so destructive the family did not dare to leave their shelter.
"The next morning I saw my hut totally razed to the ground and there was nothing left," she said, wiping a tear from her left eye with the edge of her dirty sari.
In Rajahmundry, 70 kms (45 miles) away, residents bemoaned the devastation of the settlement, which they call a cradle of Telugu culture. Telugu is the main language of Andhra Pradesh.

Acres of rice and coconut fields were still submerged after two- and three-metre (seven- and 10-foot) tidal waves hit the area. Vultures hovered over dead cattle floating in the canal along the main road, and uprooted trees were visible for miles.
Villagers helped police clear dozens of trees that had fallen across the road, their axes flashing in the sunlight as they hacked century-old banyan and tamarind trees into firewood.
Ramakrishna, 30, said he spent Wednesday night struggling with a big coconut tree that crashed onto his home.
"Then I discovered my shop in five feet of water the next morning," he told Reuters. "All my stocks of cigarettes and biscuits were destroyed."
Authorities estimated 1,400 trees and perhaps 10,000 acres of coconut groves had been destroyed.

"The economy of the whole area is dominated by the coconut tree," said one official. "The fruit is a staple of the cuisine. The water is a drink, the oil is exported. The coarse husk is used for matting. The tree trunks are used as props."
"The tree is our mother," said Ramakrishna. "Now, not one of these trees is usable. They will all have to be replanted."
Officials estimate the winds felled 20,000 electric poles. "It will take 15 days to restore" power to the area, one said.
And there has been no word at all from the submerged village of Bhairavpalem nearby, where 1,000 people lived. "There's no trace of the village," one official said. "It's out of contact."
